rationale: A wins because it changes protagonists without trying to flatter Warby. "What 40 chain optometry clinics mean for the independent eye doctor down the street" is a real hostile-but-reportable lens; B's "Warby Parker bets its next 40 stores on the optometrist, not the eyewear wall" is solid but leans on invented incumbent framing and stays closer to a company strategy note. The difference is proof discipline: A makes the holes the story; B decorates some holes with LensCrafters/Luxottica color it was not handed.
gaps_in_A: "The DTC brand that proved you don't need stores" overclaims the supplied facts. The update supports online-versus-retail spend, not Warby having "proved" the anti-store thesis.
"Warby was the canonical case study for that thesis" is outside the supplied update. It may be true, but this exercise did not hand you that proof.
"declining to break out exam revenue" turns "not broken out" into intent. Say the company does not break it out unless you have a refusal on record.

"shift of routine vision care out of independent optometry practices and into national retail chains" is a big market thesis from one company expansion. The angle is good, but it needs outside evidence before it can carry that altitude.
gaps_in_B: "LensCrafters, EssilorLuxottica, Pearle Vision" are invented context here. The update named no competitors, so this is exactly the kind of color that can quietly get a founder in trouble.
"direct shot at the incumbents' moat" is stronger than the facts allow. You have expansion into exams, not evidence of share loss, incumbent vulnerability, or a competitive response.
"started as a glasses-by-mail disruptor" relies on outside Warby history not supplied in the update. If you use it, verify it instead of smuggling it in as assumed lore.
The set misses the sharper risk protagonist: independent optometrists and the employment/regulatory model. B asks about employed versus leased ODs, then fails to turn that into a story angle.
